blocks.prompt: Sunlight Is Hiding Colors
blocks.text: A rainbow needs two things at once. It needs rain in front of you. It needs the sun behind you. Sunlight looks white, but it is not. White light is every color mixed together. When sunlight goes into a raindrop, it bends. Each color bends by a different amount. Red bends the least. Purple bends the most. The colors spread apart, bounce off the back of the drop, and come back out. Millions of drops do this at once. Your eyes see an arc of color in the sky.

red

blocks.prompt: The Bend in the Drop
blocks.text: Sunlight looks plain and white, but it is a bundle of colors traveling together. You can only see them when something pulls them apart. A raindrop can do it. Light slows down when it moves from air into water, and slowing down makes it bend. This is called refraction. Here is the useful part. Each color bends by a slightly different amount. Red bends the least. Violet bends the most. Inside a round raindrop the colors fan out, strike the far wall, bounce back, and leave the drop spread into a band. One drop is not enough. A rainbow is millions of drops, each sending you a single color. The drops that send you red sit in one ring. The drops that send you violet sit in a slightly smaller ring. Your eye stacks the rings into an arc. That is why the sun has to be behind you and low in the sky. It is also why you can never reach the end. The rainbow is not sitting over the hill. It is built out of whatever drops happen to be at the right angle from your eyes, and it moves when you move.

blocks.prompt: Why You Cannot Share a Rainbow
blocks.text: Stand with the sun behind you while rain falls in front. Somewhere ahead, an arc of color appears. It looks like it is hanging over a particular field or a particular street. It is not. It is not anywhere at all. Sunlight is a mixture of every color. When a ray enters a raindrop it slows, bends, and the mixture fans apart, because each color bends by its own amount. The fanned light travels to the back of the drop, reflects, and exits the front. What comes out is a narrow spray of color, thrown back roughly toward the sun. The geometry is strict. Red leaves the drop at about 42 degrees from the line running from the sun, past your head, to the ground. Violet leaves at about 40 degrees. So every drop currently sitting 42 degrees from that line sends you red, and only red. Every drop at 40 degrees sends you violet. Those drops form circles around the point directly opposite the sun, and the circles are what you see. The ground hides the bottom half. From an airplane, a rainbow can be a full ring. Now the strange part. The circle is centered on a line that starts at your own eyes. Move one step to the left, and the whole rainbow moves one step with you. The person standing beside you is collecting light from a completely different set of drops. She sees her rainbow, you see yours, and the two never touch. Nobody has ever reached the end of one, because the end is not a location. It is an angle.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Bow That Belongs to One Pair of Eyes
blocks.text: A rainbow is one of the few beautiful things in nature that is also a geometry problem, and the geometry is exact. Sunlight arrives as a mixture of wavelengths that our eyes read as white. When a ray strikes a spherical raindrop it crosses from air into water and slows down, which bends it. The bend is not the same for every wavelength: short waves, which we see as violet, bend slightly more than long waves, which we see as red. That small difference is called dispersion, and it is the whole trick. The fanned light crosses the drop, reflects off the inside of the far surface, and refracts again on the way out, leaving as a thin spray of separated color. Every drop does the same thing, so the direction of that spray is fixed. Red exits at roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point, the spot directly opposite the sun from your eye. Violet exits at roughly 40. The drops that happen to sit at those angles are the only drops you see color from, and because an angle traced around a point makes a circle, the bow is a circle. The horizon usually eats the lower half of it. That geometry explains a rule most people notice without understanding. You cannot see a rainbow when the sun is high. If the sun stands more than 42 degrees above the horizon, the antisolar point sinks so far below the ground that the whole circle falls out of sight. Rainbows belong to early morning and late afternoon. Look above a bright bow and you may find a second, fainter one. That light took a longer road, bouncing twice inside each drop before escaping. Two bounces cost brightness and reverse the order, so the secondary bow shows red on the inside. Between the two bows sits a band of noticeably darker sky. No drop can send light into that gap, and it has carried a name since about the year 200: Alexander's band. One last thing worth knowing. The rainbow is not seven colors. It is a smooth, unbroken spectrum with no lines in it anywhere. Isaac Newton, who proved with prisms that white light contains the colors rather than creating them, chose to name seven because he liked the match with the seven notes of a musical scale. The bands are in our language. The gradient is what is actually in the sky.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Theodoric of Freiberg traced the light path in about 1304
Descartes calculated the 42 degrees in 1637
Newton showed white light is a mixture, not a stain
Supernumerary bows are evidence that light is a wave
Moonbows look white because rod cells cannot see color
The bow is centered on the shadow of your own head

blocks.prompt: Forty-Two Degrees: The Bow Nobody Else Can See
blocks.text: A rainbow is the rare natural spectacle that is entirely explained and still worth standing in the rain for. Everything about it is known: the angle, the mechanism, the reason for the second bow, the reason for the dark stripe between them. None of that knowledge has cost it anything. Aristotle got the first piece right around 350 BC. He noticed that a rainbow always appears at a fixed angle from the person watching it, which meant it obeyed a rule rather than a mood. He then got the mechanism wrong, deciding the light bounced off the cloud as a whole. The correction took roughly sixteen centuries. Around 1304 a German friar named Theodoric of Freiberg filled glass spheres with water, held them up to the sun, and treated each one as a giant raindrop. He traced the path: the light refracts entering the sphere, reflects once off the inner back wall, and refracts again leaving. In Persia at almost the same time, Kamal al-Din al-Farisi reached the same conclusion by the same kind of experiment, neither man knowing of the other. In 1637 Descartes did the arithmetic with the law of refraction and produced the number: about 42 degrees. Newton supplied the last piece in the 1660s, showing with prisms that white light is not pure but a mixture, and that a prism separates what is already there instead of staining what passes through. Put the pieces together and the modern account is short. Sunlight enters a spherical drop and slows, which bends it. Violet, with its shorter wavelength, bends a little more than red. The colors, now fanned, cross the drop, reflect off the far inner surface, and refract once more on exit, so each drop throws a narrow spray of separated light back toward the sun. Red leaves at roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point, violet at roughly 40. Since a fixed angle swept around a point traces a circle, the bow is a circle, and the ground simply hides its lower half. A second, dimmer bow at about 51 degrees comes from light that bounced twice inside the drop, which reverses its color order and spends much of its brightness. The band of gloom between the two, described as early as about 200 AD and named Alexander's band, is the region no drop can aim light into. This is where the rainbow stops being an object. The circle is centered on the shadow of your own head. It is drawn from your eyes outward, and the drops delivering red to you are delivering something else, or nothing, to the person a step away. Two people photographing the same bow are photographing two different bows made of different water. Nobody has failed to reach the end of a rainbow through lack of trying. The end is not a place, and there is nothing waiting there, because there is nothing there to arrive at. The theory keeps paying out. Look closely inside a sharp primary bow and you can sometimes see faint pink and green fringes tucked under the violet. They are called supernumerary bows, and ray geometry has no explanation for them at all. Thomas Young accounted for them in 1804 by treating light as a wave: paths of slightly different length through the same drop arrive out of step and interfere, reinforcing here and canceling there. Those pale fringes are the rainbow quietly confirming what light is made of. And on a night with a full moon and rain you can find a moonbow, which usually looks white, not because it lacks color but because dim light is read by the rod cells in your eyes, and rods cannot tell colors apart. The color is there. Your eyes are simply not equipped to collect it at that brightness.
